title: CALREP: temperature scaling and the overfitting penalty in data-constrained pretraining (code and results)
description:
Question

When a language model is trained for many epochs on the same data, its validation loss eventually rises. Lovelace et al. (arXiv:2605.01640) model this with an additive overfitting penalty P. How much of P disappears if each model's loss is measured after one fitted temperature, which only rescales its confidence?

Answer, on 125 of Muennighoff et al.'s public C4 checkpoints (arXiv:2305.16264; 7M–2.8B parameters, 1–64 epochs)

  • About a third: the penalty falls from 0.003633 to 0.002478, so rho = P_TS / P_raw = 0.682 (bootstrap 95% interval 0.580–0.858).
  • Fitted temperatures grow with epochs: median 1.019 for single-epoch runs, 1.113 for 16–64 epochs, maximum 1.81.
  • In the 7 cells whose loss rises after its minimum and that contain no diverged run, temperature scaling removes a median 45% of the rise (range 39–54%).
  • Other analyses leave more of the penalty: 0.811 without the 11 diverged runs, 0.77–0.87 under other penalty forms. These ratios describe scalar temperature scaling only; other recalibration methods could move them either way.
  • The preregistered hypothesis (rho ≤ 0.5 with upper bound below 0.7) was not supported: no bootstrap draw is ≤ 0.5 and 48.4% are ≥ 0.7. Rho = 0.682 includes the two runs that fail the post-hoc harness rule, which have the highest temperatures.

Status: exploratory

The preregistered check of the evaluator against published losses failed (86.4% of runs within tolerance, 95% required); the cause of the loss-dependent offset was not established. A post-hoc criterion was adopted after the check data and per-run temperatures had been seen, and before the penalty refit and rho. The preregistration, the deviation log and the results record are included byte-for-byte; errata are listed in the README. One is a substitution not logged at the time: sensitivity S3 used Muennighoff et al.'s Appendix A effective-data laws instead of the preregistered Appendix F exponent-decay law, which was not run.

Method

  • Each checkpoint scored on 1,048,576 tokens of C4 validation (1,048,064 next-token targets), split by document into halves A and B.
  • Cross-fitted temperature scaling (Ashukha et al., arXiv:2002.06470 §3.5): T fitted on one half, scored on the other.
  • Lovelace et al.'s two-phase fit run on raw and on temperature-scaled loss over the same 125 runs; stratified pairs bootstrap, 1000 resamples.
  • CPU only; no GPU.

Contents

  • README.md: summary, six figures (pipeline, temperature vs epochs, bootstrap of rho, sensitivities, per-cell loss rise, harness check) and tables.
  • results/: per-run measurements, raw evaluator outputs, fits, all 1000 bootstrap draws, sensitivities.
  • code/: evaluator, fits, figures. fetch_inputs.sh checks the pinned inputs; reproduce.sh recomputes Step 0, the run set, the per-run table, the harness check, the point fit and the sensitivities, merges the shipped bootstrap shards, and fails on any mismatch (README lists what it does not cover).
  • PREREGISTRATION.md, DEVIATIONS.md, RESULTS.md: the research record.

Use of AI tools

The question came out of an AI-assisted idea search in which language models proposed and red-teamed candidate questions and the author chose which to pursue. Claude Code (Anthropic; Opus 5.5 in the main session, Sonnet 5.5 in the cloud jobs) wrote the preregistration, the code and the research records, ran the evaluation, fits and bootstrap, and drafted the README, the figures and this description. The decisions recorded as the owner's in DEVIATIONS.md (D6, D7) and the compute approvals were the author's. OpenAI Codex reviewed the code during development; each of its comments was fixed or answered. Before release, the package was reviewed by Claude Opus 5.5 and by GPT-6 Pro (ChatGPT), and their findings were fixed.
